title: Persistent communicating leak after collection control
fairness: The best offered answer is ERCP with transpapillary plastic stenting. The learner must distinguish a communicating stump leak from duct discontinuity, then integrate continuing output with a contracted, already drained cavity. Drain exchange and reconstruction represent different interpretations of those findings.
Duct continuity and collection control are necessary observations, not gratuitous answer labels. This is a high-yield postoperative bile-leak decision; difficulty is moderate rather than hard.
The first node is self-contained and does not require its later update. Its explanation does not disclose the later catheter displacement, although it primes the collection-versus-duct distinction.

Review scope: all 19 proposed nodes, comprising four rewrites and 15 new items, were assessed from candidate visible fields and preceding visible feedback. Seventeen kept records, 18 retirement proposals and five withheld teaching points were noted but not scored. No author self-check, key marker or post-answer explanation was treated as pre-answer evidence. This offline editorial review does not verify current guidelines or confer clinical approval. Runtime rendering, choice randomization and wait-preview behavior were not inspected. All drafts remain needs_clinician_review.
suggestions: For technical precision, identify the contrast-excreting MR examination as hepatobiliary-contrast MR cholangiography; ordinary MRCP does not itself show excreted contrast. The present description already supplies the necessary observed continuity and escape.

title: Recurrent collection after internal stenting

cues.phrase: the catheter pigtail lies anterior to the pocket
cues.why: Together with the visible pocket, this directly supplies the mechanical explanation and points to the only collection-directed option. It is valid clinical information, but the alternatives do not require a competing interpretation.

cues.phrase: the biliary stent draining into the duodenum without main-duct obstruction
cues.why: This explicitly neutralizes stent replacement; the preceding explanation has already said that the anatomy does not establish an indication for major reconstruction. Both distractors are therefore largely disposed of before this choice.

fairness: Image-guided drainage is the defensible best offered procedure for the newly undrained collection. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The later deterioration is coherent, and the update plus retained presentation provides enough information without remembering the first answer. However, knowing that an infected pocket needs drainage is essentially the only remaining inference; the stent and reconstruction distractors do not make it resident-level two-step reasoning.
Source control after a bile leak is high yield. Do not manufacture difficulty by removing infection findings or concealing catheter position.
suggestions: Rebuild the competition around two genuinely plausible source-control approaches, with observed collection accessibility, localization and patient condition determining the choice; retain resuscitation as shared care.
Alternatively request explicit acceptance as an easy source-control recognition item rather than presenting this exact version as a difficult resident question.

title: Referral after main-duct discontinuity
clarityIssues: The presentation calls these 'early studies' without identifying how the proximal and distal duct segments were demonstrated. A short attributed imaging report or constructed duct exhibit would make the anatomy easier to interpret.

cues.phrase: The initial hospital had no surgeon who performed complex biliary reconstruction.
cues.why: This makes transfer the obvious safe location answer against two explicitly local interventions. A reader need not interpret the duct map to reject local surgical repair.

cues.phrase: There was no continuous channel across the gap.
cues.why: The conclusion is stated after the already descriptive separate segments. Combined with the staffing sentence, the two intended inferences have largely been supplied.

fairness: HPB-center transfer with drainage maintained is the best offered plan. Avoiding a universal repair date or obligatory anastomosis is appropriate.

Major injury recognition and specialist referral are high yield, but this option set predominantly tests matching an unavailable local capability to transfer. The first node stands alone and the later peritonitis event is a coherent complication.
suggestions: Keep the genuine expertise constraint, but place specialist involvement in shared context and compare consequential interim care plans at the same stage.
Show the duct observations once, rather than adding an explicit discontinuity conclusion. Do not solve the difficulty problem by inventing a repair-time threshold or ranking disputed reconstructions.

title: Source control during diffuse biliary peritonitis

cues.phrase: a rigid, diffusely tender abdomen with falling blood pressure
cues.why: These essential emergency findings directly favor the only abdominal source-control operation. They should be preserved, but they make this a safety-recognition item with the present alternatives.

cues.phrase: the duct segments remain separated
cues.why: The prior node and its explanation already reject routine transpapillary stenting for this anatomy. Offering it again gives the learner a rehearsed elimination.

fairness: Urgent lavage and wide drainage is the best offered priority while resuscitation continues. Transhepatic diversion does not substitute for control of diffuse intraperitoneal contamination.

The new update changes the immediate priority coherently and is sufficient with the retained presentation. No confident clinical error is identified. The high-yield emergency is fair but easy, not two consequential independent reasoning steps.
suggestions: Seek explicit acceptance as a safety/recognition exception, retaining the warning signs and current clinical priority.

If resident-level difficulty is required, construct a genuinely competing source-control decision from observed anatomy and physiology; replacing obvious alternatives or accepting an intentional easy item is preferable to obscuring the emergency.

title: Surgical disposition after purported T1a resection
clarityIssues: The entire candidate presentation is a 43-year-old woman attending clinic after cholecystectomy. Both currentUpdate and exhibit are null. The task asks about 'current pathology and staging findings', but none are supplied.
The handoff's claim that new report tables were verified cannot substitute for an actual visible exhibit; its after-version display also says 'Exhibit: none.'
'Which surgical plan' contrasts a nonsurgical follow-up option with two completion operations. A neutral next-management task would express the intended decision more accurately.

cues.phrase: Cancer-team follow-up after cholecystectomy
cues.why: This is the only follow-up choice among two completion resections. With the pathological discriminator missing, a learner can only guess from this category outlier, rather than interpret evidence.

fairness: There is no determinable best answer from the supplied candidate fields. Tumor diagnosis, depth, represented muscle, margin status, completeness of removal and staging results are all absent.

The explanation introduces 'margin-negative lamina-propria-limited disease' only after the answer. Neither that explanation, the identifier nor the key marker may retroactively supply missing evidence.
The explanation's general T1a management principle is plausible, but its application to this patient is unsupported. The missing baseline also compromises the later pathology-addendum sequence.

T1a versus deeper gallbladder invasion is high yield. Moderate is a provisional estimate of the intended depth-and-completeness decision, not a claim that the currently unanswerable item has legitimate difficulty.
suggestions: Restore a real candidate pathology/staging exhibit before this question, including independently worded observations of malignant invasion depth, represented uninvolved muscle and relevant margins/completeness.

Ensure the actual exported visible fields contain the report, then independently re-review both this node and its later addendum. Do not pass this node based on author validation claims or facts found only in feedback.

title: Changed depth on gallbladder pathology addendum
clarityIssues: 'Deeper levels from a retained block' and 'remains negative' refer to a baseline pathology report that is absent from the candidate first node.

'Glands among smooth-muscle bundles' does not explicitly identify malignant infiltrating glands. Benign epithelial invaginations can involve the muscle, so this abbreviated observation is not a secure standalone statement of carcinoma invasion.

cues.phrase: HPB assessment for completion oncologic resection
cues.why: This broad assessment is the only general escalation option; the alternatives are surveillance or assessment for a specific duct resection explicitly disfavored by the negative duct margin. It is also broader than, and potentially overlaps, assessment of extrahepatic duct resection.

cues.phrase: Completely removed, margin-negative lamina-propria-limited disease generally permits cancer-team follow-up after cholecystectomy.
cues.why: The preceding explanation teaches the depth-dependent follow-up rule. The later update supplies muscle involvement, leaving an obvious switch to the only broad escalation rather than a distinct difficult decision.

fairness: If the glands are confirmed invasive adenocarcinoma, renewed HPB assessment is a reasonable best next action. This does not establish that one definitive completion operation is mandatory for every T1b patient.
As written, the node depends on preceding feedback for a cancer baseline and does not fully stand alone. Its generic-versus-specific assessments are not cleanly mutually exclusive alternatives.

Depth-driven reassessment is high yield, but the current referral-versus-surveillance set is easy once the intended malignant diagnosis is assumed. No disputed T1b operation should be silently converted into a certain rule.
suggestions: Restore the earlier report and identify the new finding as malignant infiltrating glands, using reviewed pathological wording that distinguishes invasion from benign gland displacement/invagination.

Compare equally specific next actions at the same decision stage, and supply a meaningful remaining management discriminator. If evidence cannot support a closer procedural ranking, retain the clinical uncertainty and seek acceptance for a simpler reassessment objective.

title: Extent of completion surgery for perimuscular invasion

cues.phrase: Liver-bed resection with portal lymphadenectomy
cues.why: This key is assembled from majority option components: liver-bed resection occurs twice, portal lymphadenectomy occurs in all three, and omission of bile-duct resection occurs twice. It is also the shortest unextended operation. A component-convergence attack identifies it without interpreting tumor depth.

fairness: The best offered operation is liver-bed resection with portal lymphadenectomy. Depth supports completion oncologic surgery, while clear duct margins and absent liver/major vascular involvement limit the required extent. These are two consequential considerations and a high-yield distinction.

The presentation is sufficient for the offered comparison, and the explanation appropriately avoids claiming that major hepatectomy or routine duct resection is necessary. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.
The first node stands alone. Its explanation already teaches that duct extent follows margins, substantially scaffolding the next node.
suggestions: Rebuild the option set around independent credible planning errors rather than one core operation and two larger additions. Include an appropriate undertreatment competitor if it fits the tested stage, and check component convergence again.
Retain the necessary margin and invasion observations; do not remove them merely because they explain why a more extensive operation is unnecessary.

title: Additional resection for a positive duct-wall site
clarityIssues: The new positive frozen section follows an earlier negative cystic-duct margin. This can be coherent, but identify the newly sampled remaining duct/junction tissue so the resident can distinguish a different specimen from a contradictory reading of the same margin.

cues.phrase: The proximal bifurcation and intrapancreatic distal duct are uninvolved. The liver-bed margin is clear.
cues.why: The update excludes the regions addressed by the two much larger operations, leaving a direct match between involved common hepatic duct wall and the only isolated extrahepatic duct resection.

cues.phrase: its extent follows anatomy and margin requirements
cues.why: The preceding explanation states the exact principle this follow-up repeats. New positivity changes the answer, but the sequence reduces the task to applying the just-taught site-to-resection rule.

fairness: Extrahepatic bile-duct resection with hepaticojejunostomy is the best offered site-directed extension. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified in that comparison.

The updated report plus retained presentation is sufficient, apart from specimen-orientation clarity. The alternatives address explicitly uninvolved anatomy, so this high-yield margin principle is easy rather than an independent two-step management problem.
suggestions: Identify the new specimen and relationship to the previous margin explicitly.

Use a distinct consequential clearance decision supported by a specimen map, or reduce the preceding answer-specific teaching. Compare clinically plausible extensions at the same site; do not conceal required proximal/distal boundaries to create artificial difficulty.

title: Treatment of a longstanding extrahepatic duct cyst

cues.phrase: fusiform enlargement of the extrahepatic duct
cues.why: Only 'Extrahepatic cyst excision and hepaticojejunostomy' repeats the named anatomical territory. The stem also says intrahepatic ducts are normal, making the left-hepatectomy alternative poorly competitive.

cues.phrase: no obstructing stone, stricture or solid nodule
cues.why: Together with the long extrahepatic distribution, this removes a plausible obstructive reason for the offered distal sphincterotomy. Both distractors target locations/problems not represented.

fairness: Extrahepatic cyst excision with reconstruction is the best offered treatment for the described congenital distribution. No confident clinical error is identified.

This standalone item supplies a recognizable type I pattern and asks for its customary operation. The two nominal steps are diagnosis recognition followed by associated-treatment recall, without a consequential competing patient factor.
Choledochal cyst classification and treatment are high yield. The longitudinal ultrasound can support congenital origin, but does not rescue the weak alternatives.
suggestions: Build a patient-specific anatomical or treatment-stage distinction that changes an otherwise plausible plan, using a clinician-supported comparison.
Replace the normal-left-liver resection foil with a credible same-stage error. Do not add disputed thresholds or a tenuous procedure comparison merely to make the item harder.

title: Initial tissue acquisition for a distal duct stricture

cues.phrase: EUS-guided sampling plus ERCP-based sampling
cues.why: The key combines both methods that appear separately as the other answers. It is the uniquely comprehensive 'both' response, allowing a test-wise choice without interpreting jaundice, location or pancreatic imaging.

cues.phrase: Cross-sectional staging has been completed before an endoscopic plan is chosen.
cues.why: This sentence supplies the workup sequence instead of testing it and does not discriminate among the three offered sampling plans.

fairness: Combined EUS- and ERCP-based tissue acquisition is a plausible preferred approach for this stated distal-stricture profile. No confident clinical inaccuracy is asserted; its exact guideline-specific preference was not independently verified offline.
The candidate is self-contained, but comparison of a combined plan against each component is not two consequential reasoning steps.

Biliary malignancy workup is important; this exact universal-looking combination preference is more specialized endoscopy guidance than a clearly top-priority general-surgery board distinction. The highYield rating is a qualitative scope judgment, not a measured exam-frequency claim.
The explanation establishes the initial sampling strategy but does not directly disclose the later cholangioscopy answer.
suggestions: Choose a concrete sampling target/route decision that depends on the observed anatomy, and compare equally complete plans rather than 'A plus B' versus A versus B.
Have the clinician verify the precise population and strength of the combined-sampling recommendation before scoring a categorical preference. Avoid expanding the item with decorative staging detail.

title: Persistent stricture after inadequate tissue sampling
clarityIssues: The update says EUS found no pancreatic or nodal target, but does not say that the duct narrowing itself was sampled. 'Repeat EUS needle sampling at the duct narrowing' therefore presupposes a prior procedure not established by the visible record.

cues.phrase: Repeat brush cytology of the same stricture
cues.why: Both distractors start with 'Repeat' and revisit the initial modalities, while cholangioscopy is the only novel technique. Novelty alone points toward the key after an update describing failed/inadequate initial sampling.

fairness: Persistent abnormal imaging plus inadequate samples supports further targeted acquisition; fibrosis in an inadequate specimen does not establish benign disease. Interpreting adequacy and then selecting a sampling approach can be a meaningful two-step, high-yield decision.

Cholangioscopy-guided biopsy is a defensible next approach. However, absence of a pancreatic or nodal target does not itself rule out EUS sampling of duct-wall thickening, and inadequate brushings do not make every improved repeat-sampling strategy wrong. The current record does not cleanly resolve the closest alternative.

The sequence follows the first node coherently. The later update contains the relevant prior methods and results, so it can stand without recalling the earlier selected option, once the EUS chronology is clarified.
suggestions: State what EUS actually visualized and sampled at the duct lesion, including any relevant technical limitation, without inventing a failed procedure.

Compare equally credible targeting strategies and specify what changes between attempts. Remove the unique-new-method versus two unchanged-repeat-method shortcut, while preserving the inadequate-sample observations.
Obtain clinician adjudication of the specific cholangioscopy-versus-repeat-EUS ranking for this distal lesion.

title: Primary-tumor sampling while transplant remains possible
fairness: ERCP brushings with intraductal forceps biopsies is the best offered primary-lesion sampling route. The resident must recognize the perihilar target, then consider the consequences of a transperitoneal primary-tumor needle route for a possible curative/transplant pathway.

The explicit primary-lesion target prevents inappropriate extrapolation from permitted nodal sampling. Transplant evaluation is a necessary constraint, not an unfair synonym for the answer. The ERCP-versus-two-needle-method pattern does not identify the preferred route without clinical knowledge.
This is a high-yield biopsy-route hazard. The explanation appropriately distinguishes primary sampling from sampling every node and does not claim actual transplant eligibility.

The first node stands alone. Later confirmed malignancy and selection of resection can follow evaluation of several curative options; the earlier explanation does not reveal the later drainage territory.

title: Initial drainage territory before right hepatectomy

cues.phrase: leaving the left liver
cues.why: The author explicitly computes the future remnant immediately before a left-versus-right-versus-both choice. It duplicates the inference from the planned right hepatectomy and favors the exact left-system label.

fairness: Given an already selected preoperative drainage strategy and no infected competing territory, targeting the left future remnant is the defensible best offered initial territory. No confident clinical error is identified.
The update is coherent after diagnosis and provides the resection plan independently of the first answer. Keeping the decision to drain in shared context appropriately narrows the task.

Future-remnant drainage is high yield, but the current item supplies the remnant and asks for one associated territory. Removing the explicit left-liver phrase alone would still leave mostly a single-rule application.
suggestions: Remove the redundant computed remnant, then add a clinically supported, consequential territory-selection problem that requires interpretation of a duct/drainage map and current findings.
Keep infection and planned-resection information needed for fairness; do not create difficulty by hiding whether another territory needs source control.

title: Endoscopic treatment of a traversable postoperative stricture

cues.phrase: The HPB team attributes it to the prior operation and is selecting an endoscopic treatment course.
cues.why: Both the benign postoperative interpretation and treatment modality have been selected for the learner, leaving a familiar device rule rather than the proposed anatomy-to-treatment reasoning.

cues.phrase: Temporary multiple plastic biliary stents
cues.why: The key is framed as temporary against explicitly 'Permanent' metal stenting and a sphincterotomy 'without stricture stenting'. Duration and omission wording make the alternatives look deliberately unsafe or incomplete.

cues.phrase: Papillary sphincterotomy without stricture stenting
cues.why: The label advertises failure to treat the named stricture rather than simply naming a plausible competing plan.

fairness: Temporary multiple plastic stents is the best offered course for the accepted benign traversable stricture. The explanation correctly limits the comparison and acknowledges removable covered metal stents as another strategy rather than claiming plastic superiority over every device.
Benign-stricture stent selection is high yield, but this is easy single-rule recall after the team has already supplied diagnosis and modality. The first node stands alone.

Scar without atypia and absence of a mass do not, by themselves, definitively exclude malignancy; the explicit HPB attribution permits this treatment question, but feedback should not teach those tests as universally conclusive.
suggestions: Use neutral procedure labels and replace the deliberately incomplete papillary option with a real clinical competitor.

Choose a supported patient/anatomical factor that changes a plausible endoscopic strategy, or retain this as an explicitly accepted basic device-safety item. Do not rank plastic against covered metal stenting without a defensible patient-specific reason.

title: Definitive care after recurrent nontraversable stricture
clarityIssues: The original lesion is a short mid-duct narrowing, whereas the later lesion is a long high-duct scar. Progression is possible, but identify whether this is extension of the same stricture or a new site and clarify the intervening treatment course.
The phrase 'Years later' needs a clear historical-review anchor so the retained age and original clinic encounter are not read as the time of every subsequent event.

cues.phrase: At two expert ERCP attempts a guidewire could not cross it.
cues.why: This explicitly defeats 'Another transpapillary plastic-stent course'. The remaining nonsurgical alternative is framed as permanent external drainage in an active recovered patient, making reconstruction the only affirmative definitive solution.

cues.phrase: Permanent external transhepatic drainage
cues.why: The absolute duration makes this a weak long-term competitor instead of a realistic percutaneous treatment strategy.

fairness: Specialist evaluation for hepaticojejunostomy is the best offered definitive treatment after infection control and failed expert endoscopic traversal. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The update supplies the failed procedures, controlled infection and patient fitness without requiring the earlier answer. It therefore largely stands alone, although the changed anatomy and chronology need clarification.
Failure of endoscopic treatment followed by reconstructive evaluation is high yield, but the option set tests an obvious escalation rule rather than two consequential unresolved steps.
suggestions: Clarify lesion progression, intervening stent treatment and the dates/ages of the reviewed records.

Compare genuine remaining definitive strategies with patient-specific reasons for their ranking, rather than unchanged failed ERCP and permanent external drainage. If that comparison requires evidence not available for this draft, retain a simpler explicitly accepted escalation objective.

title: Imaging a possible combined vascular and biliary injury
fairness: Multiphasic contrast-enhanced CT is the best offered next study when both a collection and unresolved hepatic arterial flow require assessment. The learner must distinguish an unestablished arterial signal from a proven occlusion, then select imaging that addresses the broader structural question rather than only bile leakage.

The stability statement provides a legitimate timing boundary. Neither 'hepatic' nor 'contrast' uniquely identifies the key, and the imaging labels are parallel. MR cholangiography and scintigraphy are plausible bile-focused errors.
Recognizing associated vascular injury during bile-duct-injury evaluation is high yield. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified in the offered modality comparison.
The first node stands alone; its explanation does not disclose whether a subsequently documented arterial occlusion warrants repair or resection.

title: Preserved hepatic enhancement despite arterial occlusion
clarityIssues: 'Early records' and 'immediate' do not establish the interval from injury recognition or the repair-relevant arterial anatomy. Those details can matter when considering selected arterial reconstruction.
'Monitor hepatic perfusion' is a broad surveillance instruction, while the other options name operations; the specific observation/follow-up action is not defined.

cues.phrase: The HPB team is planning staged biliary treatment.
cues.why: The key repeats 'during staged biliary care', while the alternatives disrupt that already announced plan. This wording can select the conservative option before interpreting the perfusion findings.

cues.phrase: enhancement throughout the right liver without necrotic areas
cues.why: This necessary observation strongly rejects the hepatectomy foil. With the only other competitor framed as immediate reconstruction, the generic monitoring answer becomes the conspicuously cautious choice.

fairness: Distinguishing arterial occlusion from current hepatic nonviability and applying the perfusion findings to management is a potentially meaningful two-step problem. Preserved enhancement argues against automatic hepatectomy.

I cannot confidently establish an exclusive surveillance-versus-reconstruction key from these details. Preserved portal flow and current enhancement do not alone settle every selected acute arterial-repair decision or eliminate later ischemic biliary complications. This is an uncertainty requiring HPB review, not a claimed factual error.

The explanation itself appropriately calls this a low-certainty boundary. Its precise repair ranking is more specialized and context-dependent than a clearly common board decision, although recognition of dual hepatic inflow is foundational.
The later CT result follows the first imaging choice coherently and the update supplies the findings needed to understand the perfusion question independently.
suggestions: Remove the answer-specific announcement of staged care, and specify the injury chronology/anatomy necessary for a clinician-supported comparison without inventing a universal time cutoff.
Name concrete, comparable management plans. Obtain HPB adjudication of the exact arterial-repair alternative before treating surveillance as the sole best answer.

If the exclusive management ranking cannot be supported, hold that teaching point or narrow the question to what the observed perfusion does and does not establish, while acknowledging its simpler difficulty.

title: Durable drainage of metastatic distal obstruction

cues.phrase: ERCP with serial plastic biliary stent exchanges
cues.why: The distractor highlights its repeated procedural burden, while the metal-stent option is presented as a single intervention. This adds a wording advantage to a familiar device-selection rule.

fairness: A self-expanding metal stent is the best offered initial drainage strategy for the stated metastatic distal malignant obstruction. The explanation compares metal with repeated plastic stenting without asserting superiority of covered over every other metal device.

Malignancy, metastatic status, a single distal obstruction and the decision to drain are already established. No curative alternative is offered, so inferring palliative intent is not a second consequential scored step; the remaining task is standard metal-versus-plastic/bypass selection.
This is high-yield general-surgery content, but easy in its current form. The first node stands alone and its explanation does not teach the later failed-access rescue route.
suggestions: Use parallel labels for the endoscopic options and move comparative exchange burden to feedback.

Add a genuine, sourced patient or anatomical consideration that changes the drainage strategy, or seek acceptance for a focused easy palliation item. Do not invent a survival threshold or add another confirmation of an already declared palliative goal.

title: Rescue drainage after inaccessible papilla
fairness: EUS-guided drainage is a defensible best offered rescue approach at an experienced center after ERCP access failure in malignant distal obstruction. The learner must recognize that the failed route is papillary access, then integrate accessible stomach, dilated left ducts, stability and expertise when comparing alternative routes.

Percutaneous drainage remains a credible alternative, not an intrinsically wrong procedure. The explicit availability of expertise in both routes avoids making capability alone uniquely select EUS. The wording and explanation should preserve this preferred-versus-only-possible distinction.

The exact contemporary recommendation favoring EUS over percutaneous rescue was not independently source-verified in this offline review; no confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The existing exact-version claim and clinician review remain necessary before clinical approval.

Rescue drainage after failed ERCP is a useful high-yield management sequence, though the advanced endoscopic details are less foundational than initial decompression. Difficulty is moderate, not hard.

The update coherently follows attempted ERCP and contains the cause of failure. With the retained presentation, it stands without remembering the earlier selected stent; the preceding explanation does not disclose this rescue answer.
suggestions: A lead-in asking for the preferred initial rescue approach would express the ranking more precisely than simply asking which procedure to 'discuss'. Keep percutaneous drainage acknowledged as a valid fallback.
